\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
Table~\ref{tab:n20} gives the median nRMSE of every strategy on every model
at $N=20$, Table~\ref{tab:tests} the paired comparisons and
Fig.~\ref{fig:relative} the same relative to the Mat\'ern ARD GP with
confidence intervals.

\subsection{GP specification and variable transformation}
Estimating the kernel amplitude and one length scale per input (Mat\'ern ARD
versus the original kernel) reduced the nRMSE on eight of the eleven
analytical models, by factors of 0.14 (physics) to 0.71 (piston), and did
not change it on the plume (both input models) and Ishigami models, where neither kernel can resolve the response
with 20 runs. On the physics model the original kernel, with its amplitude
fixed at the variance of the standardised output, cannot represent a
quadratic bowl whose values far exceed one standard deviation and reverts
towards the mean between runs. Estimating the amplitude alone reduced the
median nRMSE from 0.59 to 0.033, eighteen-fold; the earlier analysis had
attributed this error to the size of the input domain
(Section~\ref{sec:earlier}).

Fitting on the log scale, with log-transformed positive inputs, reduced the
nRMSE on all eight analytical models with positive outputs, by factors of 0.11
(borehole) to 0.75 (piston); all eight reductions remain significant
after the Holm adjustment. The GP then interpolates a nearly additive function
of the log inputs, which is what products and power laws such as the
plume, borehole and OTL formulas become.

Adding a quadratic trend to the GP reduced the nRMSE on the physics model
by a factor of 400, to the level of the sparse PCE, and changed it by
less than 0.5\% on nine of the other ten models. The exception is the OTL
circuit with 20 inputs, where the trend made the GP 1.6 to 8 times worse in
12 of the 30 designs: with 20 inputs the quadratic kernel adds 231
regression terms, which 20 runs cannot constrain. On the log scale, the
trend improved the plume models (0.42 to 0.35 with uniform inputs,
0.37 to 0.28 with GUM-type inputs), whose log concentration is close to quadratic
in the inputs, and the wing weight model (ratio 0.50), and again made the
20-input model worse (1.18). A trend is therefore a candidate to be tested
by the selection step, not a default.

\emph{Independent check of the implementations.} On the six models with
uniform inputs, our sparse PCE matched that of OpenTURNS~\cite{baudin2017}
on the same designs (median ratio of nRMSE 0.98--1.00, equivalent within
$\pm20\%$ on all six), and the Mat\'ern GP matched OpenTURNS' GP on five of
them (0.95--1.00). On the physics model the OpenTURNS GP was 9.2 times more
accurate. The cause is the upper end of the amplitude search range, $10^3$
in standardised output units, which the estimated amplitude reached in
nearly every design on that model; among all models and specifications it
was reached elsewhere only by the log-scale GP on the CFD case (3 of 6
designs checked), where widening the range changed the median nRMSE from
0.080 to 0.077. With the range widened to $10^6$, the median nRMSE on the
physics model fell from 0.033 to 0.00097 for the GP with estimated
amplitude, from 0.036 to 0.0022 with ARD and from 0.079 to 0.013 for the
Mat\'ern ARD GP. The pre-specified range thus understates the gain from
estimating the amplitude on this model, about 600-fold rather than
eighteen-fold, which strengthens the conclusion that the earlier failure
was an artefact of restricting this hyperparameter; the GP with a quadratic
trend (0.00018) remains the most accurate GP there. Universal kriging with
a full quadratic basis (OpenTURNS; $1+d+d(d+1)/2$ coefficients estimated by
generalised least squares) was 1.3--3.3 times less accurate than the
kernel-form trend used here on five of the six models, and
PC-Kriging~\cite{schobi2015}, the GP with the selected sparse PCE basis as
trend, was not more accurate than the candidate chosen by LOO error on any
of them.

\subsection{Sparse PCE and committees}
Sparse PCE matched the trend GP on the physics model and the Mat\'ern GP on
the Ishigami model, and was 1.2 to 3.8 times worse than the GP on the other
nine models; with 20 runs, the corrected LOO error selects low-degree
expansions that cannot follow the borehole, OTL and flood responses as
closely as the GP. On the log scale it was 1.1 to 12 times worse, with one
exception: on the wing weight model, a product of power laws that is
nearly linear in the log inputs, the log-scale sparse PCE was better than
the log-scale GP (ratio 0.72).

The CV-weighted committee was never better than the GP with a quadratic
trend on the same design. It tied on six models and was 1.5 to 2.4 times
worse on the other five: the borehole (both input models), OTL, wing weight
and flood models. Its
advantage on the physics model in the earlier analysis is entirely that of
its degree-2 PCE member, which the trend GP reproduces (ratio 1.00). CV
weighting remained necessary for a committee: it was never worse than
uniform averaging and better on seven models, by up to three orders of
magnitude on the physics model, where uniform averaging dilutes the exact
member with poor ones.

\subsection{Adaptive and targeted designs}
Space-filling adaptive designs gave no consistent gain at $N=20$. Adding
runs at the largest GP posterior SD never changed the nRMSE significantly
(ratios 0.86--1.22). The adaptive committee helped on the physics, borehole,
OTL, wing weight and 20-input OTL models (0.60--0.80) and hurt on the
plume model (1.25), where its estimate of $P(C>\mathrm{IDLH})$ was off by a median of 0.17, against 0.02
for the passive committee. The spectral criterion UEigV was never better
than plain committee variance and was worse on three models (1.26--1.72).

Targeting the threshold changes the picture for exceedance probabilities.
AK-MCS reduced the median absolute error of $P(Y>T)$ significantly in 8 of
the 19 comparisons, by factors of 0.11 to 0.47, and was never significantly
worse. The largest gains were on the piston model (0.0099 to 0.0014 on the
log scale), the borehole model (0.0091 to 0.0009 on the raw scale) and the
GUM-type input models. Targeting comes at a cost elsewhere: on the
Ishigami model the AK-MCS design raised the median error of the propagated
mean from 8.5\% to 28\%, because its runs cluster near the threshold.
Where the physical threshold lies in the bulk of the distribution (the
IDLH on the plume models and the CFD case), targeting the reference 95th
percentile instead reduced the error of $P(Y>y_{0.95})$ on the log scale by
median factors of 0.68 (plume) and 0.55 (plume with GUM-type inputs), but
neither reduction survived the Holm adjustment, and on the CFD case it made
no difference (0.95).

\emph{What the comparisons without a difference show.} Of the 228 paired
comparisons, 105 showed no significant difference after the Holm
adjustment. Of these, 55 were equivalent within $\pm20\%$ and 24 within
$\pm10\%$; the rest are inconclusive with 30 seeds. The statements of no
gain above are equivalences where they concern the committee against the
GP with trend (6 of its 7 ties), the quadratic trend on responses without
one (9 of 10) and the kernel specification on the plume (both input
models), Ishigami and CFD models (4 of 4), but only in part for the GP-SD design (14 of 27), whose
effect varies too much between designs for 30 seeds to show either a gain
or its absence in the other 13 cases. All 12 non-significant comparisons of
AK-MCS are inconclusive rather than equivalent.

\subsection{Propagated quantities}
Table~\ref{tab:prop} gives the validation errors of the reported quantities
for the GP recommended for each model and for the committee. With the
recommended GP, the 95th percentile was within 0.2\% (OTL, flood) to 16\%
(Ishigami) of the reference, and $P(Y>T)$ within 0.0013 to 0.036 of its
reference value. The committee's 95th percentile was off by 6.3--31\% on
seven of the eleven models. At the IDLH threshold of the plume
model, the log-variable GP estimated $P(C>210\,\mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}})=0.123$
with a median absolute error of 0.009, against 0.023 for the raw-variable
GP.

\subsection{Selecting the surrogate from the runs alone}
\label{sec:res-select}
The procedure of Fig.~\ref{fig:flowchart} fits the candidates (Mat\'ern GP,
GP with quadratic trend and sparse PCE, and their log-scale versions for
positive outputs) and keeps the one with the smallest LOO RMSE, computed on
the original scale of $Y$ from the $N$ runs alone. Applied to every seed,
this choice had a median nRMSE between 1.000 and 1.044 times that of the
best candidate in hindsight on the eleven analytical models, and was the best
candidate itself in 27--77\% of seeds; the largest shortfalls were on the
Ishigami and plume models, where several candidates are almost equally
poor or equally good. Relative to always using the Mat\'ern GP, the
selection reduced the nRMSE by a factor of 500 on the physics model (where
it chose the sparse PCE or the trend GP), by factors of 0.12--0.84 on the
models with positive outputs (choosing a log-scale GP in most seeds), and
left it unchanged on the flood and Ishigami models. On the 20-input model it
never chose the trend GP that overfits there, and on the wing weight model
it chose the log-scale sparse PCE in 9 of 30 seeds. The selection step
therefore recovers practically all of the benefit of the right
specification without access to the true model.

\subsection{Dependence on the number of runs}
\label{sec:res-budget}
Fig.~\ref{fig:budget} repeats the main strategies with $N=10$, 40 and 80
runs on the eight models with uniform inputs. The ranking of the
specifications is stable: the original kernel stays the worst GP at every
budget, and the benefit of the log scale grows with $N$, from factors of
0.62--1.00 at $N=10$ to 0.10--0.48 at $N=80$ on the six positive models,
because the transformed response is smooth enough to be learned to high
accuracy once the runs resolve it. Sparse PCE remains best on the physics
model at every budget (at $N=10$ it already has an nRMSE of
$1.6\times10^{-4}$, against 0.97 for the Mat\'ern GP) and worse than the GP
on most of the others.

The verdict on space-filling adaptive designs depends on the budget. At
$N=10$ and 20, adding runs at the largest GP posterior SD never helped
significantly. At $N=40$ and 80 it reduced the nRMSE on the physics
(0.22--0.43), borehole (0.77), OTL (0.75 at $N=80$), piston (0.81--0.87),
wing weight (0.81 at $N=40$) and 20-input OTL (0.83 at $N=80$) models,
which are smooth and on which the GP's uncertainty is informative once its
hyperparameters are well determined, but increased it on the plume model
(1.19 at $N=40$), whose error concentrates in the high-concentration corner
that the posterior SD does not single out, and on the wing weight model at
$N=80$ (1.93). The
adaptive committee was better than the passive one at $N=40$ on the
physics and borehole models (0.94 and 0.50), no different elsewhere, and
no better at $N=10$.
Adaptive selection is thus worth considering when the budget is several
times the number of inputs, but not as a remedy for very small budgets,
when the surrogate's own uncertainty is itself poorly estimated.
